bp: The object in this talk is not one search engine trick, but the changing idea of what the Web is supposed to succeed at. In the early Web, a person usually came with a fairly direct need: find a document, follow a link, reach a page that contains relevant information. Success could be imagined like a library desk working well: the right material appears quickly. As the Web became crowded with many kinds of content and many styles of interaction, that definition became too narrow. A person might not only want a page; they might want help deciding, learning, buying, being entertained, trusting a source, or returning to a service because it keeps proving useful. The talk serves the practical question of how online systems should be designed and judged when relevance is no longer only about one document matching one query, but about an experience that unfolds over time.
wh: The hard part is that the old target was much easier to see than the new one. If a search system returns a document that matches a query, evaluators can often judge the match directly. They can ask whether the page contains the needed information and whether it appeared high enough in the list. Experience is less tidy. Attention, engagement, satisfaction, trust, context, and longer-term value are spread across repeated visits and changing intentions. A click can mean interest, confusion, habit, boredom, or manipulation by a catchy title. A long visit can mean deep value, or it can mean the person is stuck. Once Web systems begin optimizing for experience, the measurement itself can reshape design: platforms may rank, surface, and structure content to increase the signals being watched. The tension is that richer goals better match real user life, but they are also harder to measure honestly and easier to confuse with short-term attention.
naive: A smart beginner would keep the early Web scorecard and simply make retrieval better. Build a large index of documents, compare the user's words with page words, count links or popularity as extra evidence, and put the most relevant pages first. If users click a result, treat that as proof that the system succeeded. This works for many direct information needs, but it fails once users expect the Web to understand purpose, setting, and trust. Two pages can both match the words while serving different intents. A user may click the first result because it is visible, not because it is satisfying. A platform can win the click while leaving the person misled, distracted, or underserved. The beginner's score measures an isolated access moment, while the modern Web often needs to measure whether the interaction produced durable value.
ap: The talk's central move is historical reframing. It says that Web evaluation did not merely add more metrics to the old retrieval task; the underlying target moved. Relevance began as a relation between a query and a document, then broadened into a relation among a person, an intent, a context, a source, and an interaction over time. That shift explains why modern Web systems care about engagement, satisfaction, trust, and sustained value, not just whether a page is reachable. It also explains why large-scale machine learning and generative models fit the current moment: they can support more interactive, adaptive, intent-aware experiences than static ranked lists alone. The point is not that retrieval disappeared. Retrieval remains a foundation. The point is that retrieval became one part of a larger design question: how should a Web system organize information and interaction so that people experience continuing usefulness rather than one-off access?
mech: The mechanism in this work is conceptual rather than an algorithm with a training loop. The input is the history of Web systems and the changing evidence used to judge them: documents, hyperlinks, queries, ranked results, clicks, repeated visits, attention, engagement, satisfaction, trust, and now AI-supported interaction. The first transformation is to separate the early target from the later target. Early systems turned a user's request into a ranked list of documents, then judged success by efficient access to relevant information. The second transformation is to notice what content abundance changed. When many pages can answer a request, the system must decide which source, format, order, and interaction best fits the person's intent and context. The third step is to widen the evidence. Instead of treating one click or one relevance label as enough, the system reads longer traces: whether people remain satisfied, whether they trust what they see, whether the platform sustains value across sessions, and whether interaction helps them express intent more precisely. The fourth step is to connect this widening to AI. Generative models can converse, adapt, and produce answers, so evaluation must ask whether the experience is grounded, useful, trustworthy, and valuable over time. The output is a framework for reasoning about Web success as an evolving measurement problem.
math: The main mathematical idea is ranking, but ranking has changed its object. In the early version, the candidates were documents and the score asked, in effect, which document should stand above which other document for this query. A score is only a handle for sorting; it compresses many reasons into one order so the system can choose what gets attention. In the experience-centered version, the candidate is partly the whole interaction: which result, answer, feed item, format, or next step should be shown so the person receives value over time. That requires aggregation, meaning the system combines many small signals from repeated behavior into a broader judgment. It also requires probability, in the plain sense of estimating uncertain states from incomplete evidence: what did the user intend, were they satisfied, do they trust this source, will this interaction remain useful later? The tradeoff is measurement richness versus measurement confusion. More signals can reveal context that a relevance label misses, but they can also reward shallow attention if the system mistakes engagement for satisfaction. The math fits because Web systems must constantly sort scarce attention among too many possible pages, answers, and experiences. It is dangerous because every score chooses what the system will learn to favor.
dots: This talk connects information retrieval, ranking, recommendation, language models, and Web governance through one shared pressure: too much content and too little human attention. Retrieval papers ask how to choose useful evidence from a large collection. Recommender systems ask how to keep choosing items that fit a person's changing interests. Language-model systems ask how to make interaction more adaptive and intent-aware. Trust and misinformation work ask whether surfacing information is enough if the person cannot judge its reliability. The talk sits above these areas as a map of why their evaluation targets have expanded. It explains why a relevance score alone feels insufficient for modern search, why recommendation cannot be judged only by immediate clicks, and why AI-generated experiences raise governance questions about satisfaction, trust, and long-term value. Its neighboring idea is ranking, but enlarged from ranking documents to ranking experiences, evidence, and interaction choices.
ww: The argument works because measures are not passive labels; they shape what systems become. If builders reward fast access to relevant documents, they will improve indexing, matching, and result ordering. That made sense when the Web's central pain was finding anything useful in a growing document network. But when content abundance makes many answers available, the bottleneck moves. The person no longer needs only access; they need help choosing, interpreting, trusting, and continuing an interaction that fits their goal. A broader scorecard can therefore explain real design changes that the old scorecard cannot: personalized feeds, context-aware search, satisfaction surveys, retention measures, trust signals, and conversational AI. The historical view is stronger than a simple method comparison because it shows why the target had to move as the Web's material conditions changed. More content, more interaction modes, and higher user expectations made isolated relevance a partial measure. Experience metrics appear because the system's real job expanded from finding pages to organizing ongoing value.
po: The payoff is a clearer way to reason about Web systems today. The talk gives designers and evaluators a vocabulary for asking whether they are measuring the right thing: not only whether information was retrieved, but whether the user intent, context, satisfaction, and trust were served. It also grounds the rise of AI-enabled Web platforms in a longer history rather than treating them as a sudden break. Generative and large-scale learned systems matter here because they intensify the move toward interactive, adaptive experiences. The result is a framework for designing and governing future online systems with more awareness of what their success metrics reward.
limits: The abstract describes a historical and conceptual talk, not a controlled experiment. It does not prove that any particular satisfaction, engagement, or trust metric truly captures long-term user value. It also does not settle the conflict between helpful experience design and attention capture, where the same signals can encourage habit-forming interfaces. The argument assumes that the Web's evolution can be understood through changing goals and metrics, but different communities, countries, platforms, and user groups may experience that evolution differently. The abstract also names AI as accelerating the trend, but it does not specify which model designs, evaluation procedures, or governance rules prevent adaptive systems from optimizing the wrong signals.
